title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #12 (Hard Tier)
description: Full-length 53-question high-difficulty simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes). Elevated distractor plausibility and edge-case testing.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A streamed assistant turn opens with a `text` block at index 0 (`Let me check that order.`) followed by a `tool_use` block at index 1. To keep history compact, the handler stores only the `tool_use` block as the assistant turn, then sends the matching `tool_result`. Requests succeed, but follow-up turns sometimes repeat or contradict the earlier explanation. What does the course say about this handler?

options.text: It should store the text block and drop the `tool_use` block instead, since the `tool_result` already carries the `tool_use_id` the API needs to match.
It is correct, because text blocks in a tool-use turn are commentary that the API ignores when it reads conversation history on subsequent requests.
It should move the text block into the next user turn alongside the `tool_result`, since the user role carries everything the application sends back.
It is wrong: when a text block comes alongside a tool_use block, the full content array must be kept in history, or Claude's context is corrupted.

questions.explanation: Claude may return a text block alongside a tool_use block in the same turn. The course's block-structure table says your code must preserve the full content array, including that text block, when appending the turn to history; dropping it corrupts the context Claude relies on for follow-up turns. The tool_use block must also stay, because each tool_result has to pair with it by ID.

distractor_explanations.A: Every `tool_result` must pair with a `tool_use` block in the immediately preceding assistant turn; dropping that block fails validation.
distractor_explanations.B: The course says to preserve the full content array, including the text block; dropping it corrupts the context for follow-up turns.
distractor_explanations.C: The text is Claude's assistant output. Moving it into the user turn misattributes it and still breaks the assistant turn's content.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A streaming handler correctly waits for `message_stop` before acting. On one long request, the stream completes normally, but `message_delta` reported `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`, and the last content block is a `tool_use` whose accumulated input JSON is cut off mid-object. The handler executes the tool because `message_stop` arrived. What should it do instead?

options.text: Send a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` for the truncated call so the model reissues the complete call on its next turn without a full retry.
Execute the tool, because the course's rule is that a turn is complete and safe to act on once `message_stop` has been received for the stream.
Check `stop_reason` before running tools: `max_tokens` means generation was cut off, so the truncated call must not run; regenerate the turn.
Repair the truncated JSON by closing the open braces and execute the call with the recovered fields, since the missing fields are usually optional ones.

questions.explanation: The course's streaming rules are two-part: act only after the block closes and the message completes, and check the `stop_reason` from `message_delta` before continuing a loop. A `stop_reason` of `tool_use` means the assembled tool calls are ready to run; any other value, such as `max_tokens`, means you are on a different path and must not execute the partial call.

distractor_explanations.A: With `stop_reason: max_tokens` the model was not waiting on tool results. The turn itself is incomplete and should be regenerated.
distractor_explanations.B: `message_stop` means the stream finished, not that the model finished. `stop_reason` says which path you are on, and only `tool_use` means calls are ready.
distractor_explanations.D: Hand-repairing truncated input runs a tool with arguments the model never finished writing.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team designs a Message Batches job in which request 2 should summarize the output of request 1, and request 3 should compare both. Which TWO statements about this design are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Setting a request's `custom_id` to reference an earlier request's `custom_id` makes the batch run them as a chain, passing outputs forward.
Batch requests are processed independently, in no guaranteed order, so request 2 cannot consume request 1's output inside the same batch.
Dependent steps belong in successive batches or synchronous calls, using each result's `custom_id` to build the next stage's inputs.
Batches under 10,000 requests are processed in submission order, so a short dependent chain like this one is safe to run inside a single batch.
Requests in one batch share a conversation context, so request 2 can refer to the previous summary without restating it in its own messages.

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API processes each request asynchronously and independently, and results return in arbitrary order, so `custom_id` is how outputs are matched back to inputs. Requests cannot share state or chain within a batch. A multi-stage pipeline therefore runs as successive batches (or synchronous calls) that build each stage's inputs from the previous stage's results.

distractor_explanations.A: `custom_id` is a caller-assigned key for matching results to inputs. It creates no dependency and no ordering.
distractor_explanations.D: There is no ordering guarantee at any size; results return in arbitrary order.
distractor_explanations.E: Each batch request is a self-contained Messages request with no shared state between requests.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: An assistant turn contains three `tool_use` blocks issued in parallel. To reduce latency, the application sends the next request as soon as the first tool finishes, with a user turn holding only that one `tool_result`, and plans to send the other two results when they arrive. That request fails validation. What is the fix?

options.text: Set `disable_parallel_tool_use` so Claude issues one call per turn, because the API cannot accept results for more than one tool in a single turn.
Wait for all three tools, then return all three `tool_result` blocks together in the single user turn right after the assistant turn, each with its matching ID.
Keep sending early, but put the two pending results in the next assistant turn when they arrive, since the assistant role records what the tools returned.
Insert a placeholder assistant message after the partial user turn, so roles alternate correctly before the two remaining results are sent.

questions.explanation: The API requires every tool_use block from an assistant turn to be answered by a tool_result with a matching ID in the user turn that immediately follows. The course's loop checklist adds that all tool-use blocks from a single assistant turn must be resolved together. Sending a request while two of the three tool_use blocks are still unanswered breaks that invariant, even though the one result that was sent has the correct ID.

distractor_explanations.A: The API accepts multiple tool_result blocks in one turn. Disabling parallel calls is for genuine dependencies, not for this bug.
distractor_explanations.C: tool_result blocks always belong in the user role, and every result must be in the user turn immediately following the tool_use turn.
distractor_explanations.D: Fabricated assistant turns mean the later results no longer immediately follow the tool_use turn, and all results must be resolved together.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A nightly Message Batches job classifies product photos stored in a private bucket. Each request references its image through a URL `source` pointing to a pre-signed link that expires after 15 minutes. Many results come back errored with image-fetch failures. What is the best fix?

options.text: Avoid short-lived URLs for async work: send images as inline base64, or upload reused images once via the Files API and reference the `file_id`.
Make the bucket public for the duration of the job, so URL fetches no longer need a signature and succeed whenever each request is processed.
Resubmit the errored requests immediately as a new batch, because image-fetch failures are transient network errors that usually clear on retry.
Extend the pre-signed URL lifetime to two hours, which comfortably covers how long a typical batch takes to finish processing all of its requests.

questions.explanation: A URL source requires the image to be public, stable, and reachable at the moment Claude fetches it. The course says to skip URLs for anything behind auth or signed with a short expiry. Batch work makes this worse because requests run asynchronously, within a window of up to 24 hours. Inline base64 suits one-off images, and the Files API suits images reused across requests.

distractor_explanations.B: That exposes private data. The course points to base64 or the Files API for content you cannot guarantee is reachable.
distractor_explanations.C: The same expired URLs would fail again. The encoding method is the defect, not a transient fault.
distractor_explanations.D: Batches can take up to 24 hours. Any expiry shorter than the completion window can still fail, and short-expiry signed URLs are the case the course says to avoid.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: After a configuration change, every request from a service returns a 404 `not_found_error`, because the model string now names an identifier that does not exist on the platform. The service's retry wrapper treats every non-2xx response as retriable and backs off for several minutes per request before failing. What should change?

options.text: Keep retrying 404s with a longer backoff, because new model identifiers can take time to propagate across regions after a release goes out.
Keep 404 in the retriable set but cap it at two attempts, because the cap stops the retry budget from being exhausted by any one failure type.
Fall back automatically to the family alias whenever a 404 occurs, so requests keep succeeding while the configuration is being corrected.
Classify 404 as terminal and fail fast, surfacing the error so the bad model ID gets fixed; retrying an identical request changes nothing.

questions.explanation: The course's first question for any failure is whether retrying the identical request could plausibly succeed. Statuses like 400, 401, 403, and 404 come from the request itself, so they fail identically every time and should fail fast and be surfaced. Retrying them burns the retry budget and hides the real problem behind repeated failures.

distractor_explanations.A: A 404 is terminal in the course's taxonomy. Waiting does not make a wrong identifier valid.
distractor_explanations.B: Any retry of a terminal error wastes budget and adds latency. Terminal statuses should fail fast.
distractor_explanations.C: A silent fallback to a moving alias creates an untracked production change. Fail fast and fix the pinned ID.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A fleet of 200 workers hits a rate limit, and each 429 response includes `retry-after: 30`. The current code ignores the header and retries after 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds with no jitter, so every worker retries in lockstep and keeps hitting the limit. Which retry policy matches the course?

options.text: Wait the `retry-after` value and then retry every worker at that exact moment, since the header guarantees capacity is available for all of them.
Ignore `retry-after` and use exponential backoff with jitter, because client-side backoff adapts better than a server-supplied estimate does.
Switch to immediate retries with a higher attempt cap, since a 429 clears quickly and waiting only wastes throughput the fleet could be using.
Honor `retry-after` as the authoritative wait with jitter added, and fall back to capped exponential backoff with jitter when it is absent.

questions.explanation: For retriable rate limits, the course prescribes exponential backoff with jitter, a cap on attempts, and honoring `retry-after` when the response includes it. The header is the authoritative wait, and your own backoff is the fallback when it is absent. Jitter matters at fleet scale, because synchronized retries keep landing on the same limit.

distractor_explanations.A: Synchronized retries recreate the stampede. Jitter spreads the fleet out.
distractor_explanations.B: The course says to treat `retry-after` as authoritative when present, because the service is telling you when capacity returns.
distractor_explanations.C: Instant retries each count as another request against the same limit and deepen it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A customer runs on AWS and wants to pay through their AWS account, but their priorities are Anthropic's model IDs, Anthropic's deprecation schedule, and feature parity with the first-party API. They have no requirement that inference stay inside their AWS boundary. Which option fits best?

options.text: Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) via `Converse`, because `Converse` mirrors Anthropic's Messages API, model IDs, and lifecycle exactly.
Claude in Amazon Bedrock with a global endpoint, because the global endpoint routes to Anthropic infrastructure and therefore follows Anthropic's lifecycle.
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, because it is the AWS route with broad feature parity, and it follows Anthropic's own published retirement dates for each model.
Claude Platform on AWS: reached through the customer's AWS account with Anthropic's model IDs and lifecycle, and inference run by Anthropic.

questions.explanation: Claude Platform on AWS is reached through the customer's AWS account using Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, with feature parity to the first-party API; inference is Anthropic-operated, outside the AWS boundary. Claude in Amazon Bedrock keeps data in the AWS boundary but uses `anthropic.`-prefixed IDs and partner retirement dates. With no in-boundary requirement, Claude Platform on AWS matches these priorities.

distractor_explanations.A: The legacy integration uses InvokeModel/Converse with ARN-versioned identifiers, not Anthropic's IDs or lifecycle.
distractor_explanations.B: Global versus regional endpoints affect residency and cost, not which model lifecycle applies.
distractor_explanations.C: Bedrock pins `anthropic.`-prefixed IDs, and partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's schedule.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A German bank requires all Claude inference for a new workload to be processed within the EU. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Adding an EU region header to first-party API requests pins inference to EU data centers for that request, so no platform change is required.
The first-party API doesn't currently offer EU data residency, so EU-only requirements go to Bedrock or Vertex AI with the region pinned.
Any Claude model consumed through Microsoft Foundry in an EU Azure region satisfies EU residency, whichever hosting form the model uses.
On Bedrock, the choice of global versus regional endpoint is the primary residency control, and it can also change the cost of the workload.
Encrypting request payloads end to end satisfies residency, because the provider can no longer read the data that it processes.

questions.explanation: The course states that the direct Anthropic API does not currently provide EU data residency, so partners with EU requirements route through Bedrock or Vertex with the region pinned in client configuration. Within Bedrock, the global-versus-regional endpoint choice is the primary residency control and can affect cost. Foundry residency depends on each model's hosting form, so confirm current regional coverage at build time.

distractor_explanations.A: The course says the direct API does not currently provide EU data residency. No request header changes that.
distractor_explanations.C: Anthropic-hosted Foundry models do not satisfy EU regional residency. It has to be checked per model.
distractor_explanations.E: Residency is about where data is processed, not whether it is encrypted in transit.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team moving from the first-party API to Claude in Amazon Bedrock copies its pinned model ID string unchanged into the Bedrock client and assumes retirement dates will follow Anthropic's published deprecation schedule. Which correction does the course make?

options.text: Pin the Bedrock full model ID in the `anthropic.` prefix format (often with a regional prefix like `us.`) and confirm Bedrock's own retirement dates.
Both the ID and the lifecycle carry over unchanged, because model snapshots are identical on every platform and retire on the same date everywhere.
Bedrock ignores model ID strings and pins versions only by ARN, so the team must replace the ID with an inference-profile ARN in the client.
The ID string is right as-is, because Claude in Amazon Bedrock uses the same model ID format as the first-party API; only the retirement dates differ.

questions.explanation: The course's deployment table says Claude in Amazon Bedrock pins the full model ID in the `anthropic.` prefix format (its corrected example uses `us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8`), and that partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's schedule. Copying a first-party ID or assuming Anthropic's deprecation dates both carry first-party assumptions onto a platform that follows its own conventions.

distractor_explanations.B: Partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's, so the lifecycle has to be confirmed per platform.
distractor_explanations.C: ARN-versioned identifiers belong to the legacy InvokeModel/Converse integration. The Messages API integration pins the prefixed full model ID.
distractor_explanations.D: Anthropic's own ID format is how Claude Platform on AWS pins models. Claude in Amazon Bedrock uses the `anthropic.` prefix.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team wants to adopt a newer pinned model snapshot for a production summarizer. Which release process matches the course's deployment guidance?

options.text: Pin the new model ID, route part of the traffic to it, compare its eval against the pinned baseline, then promote or roll back, keeping the prior version.
Switch the model string to the family alias so the service always gets the newest snapshot automatically, and monitor error rates for a week.
Run the new snapshot through the unit and functional test suites, and promote it if they pass, since those suites cover the parser and response shape.
Promote the new snapshot to all traffic and delete the prior pinned ID from config, so no service can accidentally regress to the older version.

questions.explanation: The course makes the eval the deployment gate: send a new version to a portion of traffic, compare it against the pinned baseline, and promote or roll back on the result. Pin the full model ID rather than an alias, version the prompt alongside the code, and keep the prior pinned version available so a regression becomes a rollback rather than a hotfix.

distractor_explanations.B: An alias turns every upstream update into an untracked production change. Promotion should be gated on the eval.
distractor_explanations.C: Shape tests do not measure quality. Promotion is gated on the eval against the pinned baseline.
distractor_explanations.D: Deleting the prior version removes the rollback target the course says to keep.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A business sponsor's brief says only: `Help adjusters triage incoming claims faster.` Before any platform is chosen, which set of questions does the course say surfaces the infrastructure requirements that most often decide the deployment platform?

options.text: Which claim categories exist, what each triage outcome looks like, and at what point a human adjuster must approve the agent's decision.
How fast responses must be where adjusters are, how many requests at peak, where claim data must be processed, and who acts under which credentials.
Which cloud the team knows best, which SDK language it prefers, and which platform offers the lowest per-token rate for the expected volume.
Which model tier, which prompting pattern, which tool set, and which memory scope the agent should use for each kind of incoming claim.

questions.explanation: Functional requirements state what the system must do; infrastructure requirements are the non-functional constraints you derive by asking the questions the business problem implies. The course names latency (measured where the user is), scale, residency, and identity as the infrastructure requirements that most often decide the platform, and says to capture them before a platform is picked for other reasons.

distractor_explanations.A: These are functional requirements (what the system must do), not infrastructure constraints.
distractor_explanations.C: Familiarity and token price are the traps the course warns about; they are not requirements.
distractor_explanations.D: Those are design decisions that follow from the requirements, not the infrastructure requirements themselves.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: An invoice-processing accelerator is parameterized, documented, and ships with its eval suite. It passes every demo, but the first regulated customer's security review stalls. The reviewer asks what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, and what record it leaves. What was missing from the package?

options.text: A data-flow diagram of everything the asset reads and writes, since a reviewer's concern is data scope rather than any runtime record.
A hardened system prompt telling the agent never to touch sensitive data, because reviewers check prompt-level controls before anything else.
The service-account key the asset uses, committed alongside its config, so the reviewer can confirm exactly which identity the asset acts under.
The audit bundle: a statement of the data touched and the identity acted under, plus a log of what the asset did, shipped as part of the package.

questions.explanation: The course's packaging checklist has three columns for every asset type: what to parameterize, what to document, and what to bundle for audit. A regulated reviewer asks what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, and what log it leaves; an accelerator without those passes a demo and stalls at the first security review. The audit log is part of the package.

distractor_explanations.A: A diagram covers data scope only. It says nothing about the identity the asset acts under or the record it leaves of what it actually did.
distractor_explanations.B: Prompt instructions are not controls, and the reviewer asked for an inspectable record.
distractor_explanations.C: Committing a credential is a secret-handling defect, and it still answers neither the data question nor the logging question.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer's pull request to an open-source Claude tooling repository bundles a bug fix, a refactor of the module's error handling, and a new optional feature, with tests for the fix only. It has gone unreviewed for a month. What change best follows the course?

options.text: Split it so the PR does one thing (the fix), with a runnable example, a test, and a statement of assumptions; offer the rest separately.
Move the contribution to the Claude Cookbook, which accepts larger multi-part changes than individual tool repositories generally do.
Add tests for the refactor and the feature so the whole bundle is covered, then ping the maintainer again to ask for a full review.
Rebase onto the latest main and expand the PR description with the full development history, so the maintainer understands the context.

questions.explanation: A maintainer accepts what they can verify. The course lists four things that make verification possible: the code does one thing, an example shows it running, a test proves it works, and a short statement names the assumptions. A contribution the reviewer cannot verify without reconstructing intent goes to the back of the queue.

distractor_explanations.B: The Cookbook is for focused reference implementations. A fix belongs in the tool's own repository.
distractor_explanations.C: Coverage helps, but a sprawling PR still forces the reviewer to reconstruct intent. Focus is the first criterion.
distractor_explanations.D: History does not replace a focused, verifiable change. The maintainer would still have to reverse-engineer three changes.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team connects two remote MCP servers in Claude Code: the GitHub MCP server for repository tooling and the Linear MCP server for issues. Which TWO statements about authentication are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Linear's server uses OAuth: on first connection the client redirects to Linear's sign-in, and after approval a token is issued and stored without manual copying.
Because both are remote, they must use stdio transport, with authentication handled by environment variables inside the spawned subprocess.
Both servers should use OAuth, because remote HTTP servers are expected to authenticate individual users through a browser-based sign-in flow.
GitHub's PAT can be committed inline once to unblock teammates, then moved to an environment variable in a later commit after everyone has cloned.
GitHub's server takes a Personal Access Token as a Bearer header that references an environment variable, never an inline value.

questions.explanation: The course contrasts the two: the GitHub MCP server is a remote HTTP server authenticated with a Personal Access Token passed as a Bearer header, supplied through an environment variable and never committed inline to `.mcp.json`. Linear's remote server uses OAuth, where the client runs a browser sign-in and stores the issued token. Both follow the same transport and scope logic; only authentication differs.

distractor_explanations.B: Remote servers use HTTP transport. Stdio is for local subprocesses.
distractor_explanations.C: The GitHub server uses a PAT as a service credential. OAuth fits services whose authorization is tied to user identity.
distractor_explanations.D: A committed token enters repository history permanently. Overwriting it later does not remove the exposure.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A healthcare customer's security reviewer asks three questions about a Claude Code and MCP integration: where is data processed, how is tool access logged, and can an administrator lock the authentication setup so developers cannot change it during an audit window? Which answer set matches the course?

options.text: The first-party API with ZDR enabled; a PostToolUse hook for audit logging; and a user-level `~/.claude/settings.json` that IT distributes.
A region-pinned platform and regional HTTP endpoint, a PostToolUse hook logging every tool call, and enterprise managed settings nobody can override.
A region-pinned platform; a CLAUDE.md instruction telling the agent to log its tool calls; and a project `.claude/settings.json` committed to the repository.
A region-pinned platform; a PreToolUse hook that blocks tool calls during audit windows; and `.claude/settings.local.json` on each developer machine.

questions.explanation: The course maps each regulated-review question to a concrete control. Data residency comes from an HTTP endpoint in a specific region combined with a platform deployment pinned to that region. Access logging comes from a PostToolUse hook that records every tool call deterministically. Configuration lock comes from administrator-deployed managed settings that users and project files cannot override.

distractor_explanations.A: ZDR does not answer where data is processed, and user-level settings are not administrator-locked.
distractor_explanations.C: CLAUDE.md is a convention, not a deterministic log, and project settings can be overridden. The course uses hooks and managed settings.
distractor_explanations.D: Blocking is not logging, and local settings are personal overrides, not an administrator lock.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A CI job runs an Agent SDK agent on a shared build machine. The agent must load the repository's skills and CLAUDE.md, but must not pick up anything from the build user's personal `~/.claude` configuration. How should `settingSources` be set?

options.text: Explicitly to `["project"]`, so only the repository's filesystem settings load and the build user's settings are excluded.
To `["user", "project", "local"]`, which matches Claude Code CLI behavior and is the recommended setting for production jobs.
To `[]`, which isolates the run from user settings while still discovering the repository's skills automatically.
Leave it unset, because the SDK's default in non-interactive environments already loads project settings and skips user-level ones.

questions.explanation: Whether the Agent SDK loads filesystem settings such as CLAUDE.md and skills is controlled by `settingSources` (`setting_sources` in Python). The course's examples are `["user", "project", "local"]` to match CLI behavior and `[]` for full isolation, and it insists on setting the value explicitly. Selecting only the project source loads the repository's configuration without the build user's.

distractor_explanations.B: That loads the build user's personal settings, which the requirement forbids.
distractor_explanations.C: An empty list runs fully isolated with only what you pass programmatically, so the project's skills and CLAUDE.md would not load either.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says never to rely on a default: set `settingSources` explicitly and confirm behavior against the SDK reference.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team ships a Claude Code plugin named `payments` with a `run-tests` command, referenced throughout their runbooks as `/payments:run-tests`. They rename the plugin to `billing` in its manifest. A second plugin in the org also ships a `run-tests` command. What happens?

options.text: The two `run-tests` commands now collide, because automatic namespacing only applies when both plugins come from the same marketplace.
Commands keep their original `/payments:` prefix, because the namespace is fixed when the plugin is first installed and only the display name changes.
Every command becomes `/billing:<command>`, so runbooks citing `/payments:run-tests` break; the other plugin's `run-tests` stays distinct.
Commands become unprefixed `/run-tests`, and when two plugins collide, the plugin that was installed first wins the name for every user.

questions.explanation: Plugin commands are namespaced automatically: the plugin's name becomes the prefix, so `run-tests` in a plugin named `payments` is `/payments:run-tests`. That is why two plugins can ship the same command name without colliding. The course tells authors to treat the plugin name as part of the interface, because renaming the plugin renames every command it ships.

distractor_explanations.A: Namespacing applies to plugin commands regardless of marketplace, which is why both plugins can ship a `run-tests` command.
distractor_explanations.B: The plugin name is the prefix, so renaming the plugin renames every command it ships.
distractor_explanations.D: Plugin commands are always namespaced by plugin name; there is no unprefixed fallback.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: An agentic coding workload is more expensive per token on the higher model tier. Instrumentation shows the lower tier needs about three times as many turns and tool calls to finish the same tasks, and makes more wrong edits that have to be reverted. How should the team choose between tiers?

options.text: Choose the lower tier, because per-token price is the decisive cost metric, and the extra turns only affect latency rather than the bill.
Compare measured cost per completed task, including extra turns and reverted edits, plus the eval score; the pricier tier may finish cheaper.
Choose the higher tier for all coding work by default, because the most capable model is the safest choice for production workloads.
Choose the lower tier with high reasoning effort, because extra effort reliably closes the quality gap with the higher tier at lower total cost.

questions.explanation: The course notes that a higher-tier model can process a request faster and cheaper if it reaches a conclusion in fewer tokens, and that the cost of mistakes belongs in the calculation. The discipline is to make the trade-off measurable (cost per task from per-call instrumentation, plus the eval score) rather than comparing per-token prices or defaulting to the biggest model.

distractor_explanations.A: Cost is measured per task, not per token. Extra turns and reverted edits are real spend.
distractor_explanations.C: The course calls defaulting to the most capable tier the most common and expensive mistake. Decide on measurement.
distractor_explanations.D: Effort is a separate lever that adds billed thinking tokens, and nothing guarantees it closes the gap. Measure it on the eval.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A multi-tenant assistant's system prompt begins `Tenant: {tenant_name}. Today: {date}.`, followed by an 8,000-token policy manual shared by all tenants, with one cache breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. Cache reads across tenants are rare. Which restructuring follows the course?

options.text: Hash the tenant name so it is short and constant-length, which lets the cache match prefixes of equal length across tenants.
Switch to the one-hour TTL, so each tenant's version of the prefix stays cached for longer between that tenant's own requests.
Put the shared manual first (after stable tools), put the breakpoint on it, and move tenant name and date after the breakpoint.
Add a second breakpoint right after the tenant line, so the tenant-specific prefix is cached separately from the shared policy manual.

questions.explanation: Caching matches on an exact prefix, and requests are processed tools, then system, then messages. Anything that varies before the breakpoint, such as a tenant name or date at the very top, makes every tenant's prefix unique. The course's guidance is to put stable content first, mark the breakpoint after it, and place dynamic content after the breakpoint.

distractor_explanations.A: Matching is on identical content, not length; any differing characters before the breakpoint break the match.
distractor_explanations.B: A longer lifetime helps reuse within one tenant, but the shared manual is still never reused across tenants.
distractor_explanations.D: The tenant line still precedes the manual, so the manual's cached prefix includes tenant text and differs for every tenant. The fix is ordering.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team is modeling prompt-caching economics for a workload with a long, stable prefix. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A request may place up to eight breakpoints, which is why long conversations rarely need the automatic caching mode at all.
The default lifetime is five minutes and is refreshed on each cache hit, so a prefix that is reused several times a minute stays warm.
Caching is enabled with an organization-wide setting, after which every request's prefix is cached automatically with no request changes.
Cache reads are billed at roughly half the base input rate, which is the same discount the Message Batches API applies to its requests.
Writes cost more than base input (1.25x for 5-minute, 2x for 1-hour lifetimes), while reads cost about 0.1x of standard input.

questions.explanation: The course gives the pricing (writes at 1.25x for the 5-minute TTL and 2x for the 1-hour TTL, reads at 0.1x), so caching pays only when reads outnumber writes. The default lifetime is five minutes and is refreshed on each hit. Caching is turned on per request, through automatic mode or up to four explicit breakpoints.

distractor_explanations.A: The limit is four breakpoints per request.
distractor_explanations.C: There is no global switch. Caching uses automatic mode on the request or explicit `cache_control` breakpoints.
distractor_explanations.D: Reads cost about 0.1x. The roughly 50% figure is the batch discount.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer maintaining a long multi-turn chat writes code that moves an explicit `cache_control` breakpoint to the latest message on every turn, and often gets the placement wrong. What does the course recommend as the starting point for most use cases?

options.text: Automatic caching: one cache flag at the top level of the request, with the system managing breakpoints as the conversation grows.
Pin all four breakpoints permanently on the first four messages, so the earliest part of the conversation history is always cached.
Disable caching for chat and rely on the batch discount instead, since a multi-turn conversation never repeats the same prefix.
Set the one-hour TTL on the system prompt only, because conversation turns change on every request and can never be cached.

questions.explanation: The course describes two caching modes. In automatic mode you add a single cache flag at the top level of the request and the system manages breakpoints as the conversation grows; this is the recommended starting point for most use cases. Explicit breakpoints put a `cache_control` marker on a specific block when you need precise control.

distractor_explanations.B: Fixed early breakpoints cache only the start. As the conversation grows, most of the reusable prefix sits beyond them.
distractor_explanations.C: Chat history is a growing stable prefix, a strong caching candidate, and batching does not suit a live chat.
distractor_explanations.D: Earlier turns are stable once sent and are cacheable as the conversation grows. Automatic mode handles this.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A document-QA service sometimes sends requests whose inputs exceed the model's context window, and the API rejects them with a validation error before generation. The team estimates size by dividing characters by four with a generic open-source tokenizer, which also misses tool definitions and images. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Rely on the API to drop the oldest turns when the input is too large, and log a warning whenever that trimming takes place.
Send the request and, on the validation error, retry it with a lower `max_tokens`, which leaves more of the window for the oversized input.
Call `count_tokens` with the same request body, tools and images included, to get the count without inference; trim or summarize when over budget.
Keep the characters-divided-by-four heuristic but subtract a 20% safety margin, because characters per token stay stable across Claude model generations.

questions.explanation: The `count_tokens` endpoint takes the same request body as a messages call and returns the token count without running inference. The course recommends it for checking context-budget assumptions against real inputs and for gating requests that would exceed the window before they fail. Character-based heuristics are model-dependent, and the API rejects oversized input rather than trimming it.

distractor_explanations.A: The API never silently truncates input. Trimming and summarizing are the application's job.
distractor_explanations.B: When the input alone exceeds the window, no `max_tokens` value makes it fit, and retrying the identical input fails again.
distractor_explanations.D: The course says characters per token depends on the model's tokenizer and differs between generations, so measure instead.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A marketing tool on one of the newest Claude models needs five noticeably different taglines per request. The old implementation raised `temperature` to 1.0 for variety, and on the new model that request returns a 400. What is the course-aligned approach?

options.text: Call the model five times with the identical prompt at default settings, because sampling guarantees five meaningfully different taglines.
Keep `temperature: 1.0` but move it into `output_config`, where sampling controls now live for the newest generation of models.
Drop the sampling parameter and steer variety in the prompt, for example by asking for five distinct taglines with explicitly different angles.
Set `top_p: 0.95` instead of `temperature`, because only the temperature control was removed from the newest models' request schema.

questions.explanation: The course states that the newest Claude models do not accept non-default sampling parameters: setting temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400, and behavior is steered through prompting instead. Sampling still makes outputs non-deterministic, but variety you actually need, such as distinct alternatives, should be requested explicitly in the prompt.

distractor_explanations.A: Default sampling makes outputs vary but does not guarantee distinct results. Explicitly prompting for variety is the lever.
distractor_explanations.B: Sampling is not relocated. Non-default sampling parameters are not accepted on these models.
distractor_explanations.D: The newest models reject non-default temperature, top_p, and top_k alike.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: Which TWO workloads are a good fit for the Message Batches API? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A pipeline in which each document's summary must be fed into the next document's classification request.
An IDE inline-completion feature that must respond within 500 ms of each keystroke for thousands of users.
A contract summary that a user just requested and is watching for in the app, which the team would like at half price.
A weekly re-labeling of 60,000 archived support tickets where no consumer is waiting on any individual result.
A regression eval that runs a new prompt version against 3,000 graded cases as part of an offline promotion check.

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API trades latency for cost: it processes requests asynchronously, within up to 24 hours, at a lower per-token price. The course names offline pipelines, evaluation runs, and scheduled data processing as the fit, and rules out any flow where a user is waiting. Requests are independent, so dependent chains need successive batches.

distractor_explanations.A: Requests in a batch are independent, so dependent chains cannot run inside a single batch.
distractor_explanations.B: This is a real-time latency requirement. Batching is asynchronous.
distractor_explanations.C: A user is waiting, and batch processing can take up to 24 hours.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: In an orchestrator-worker research system, one subagent hits a 429 and, having no retry logic, hangs waiting on a response. The lead waits indefinitely to compile results, and the whole request times out even though the other subagents finished. What gap does the course identify?

options.text: The lead should run on a more capable model, which would recognize the stalled worker and reassign its subtask to another subagent.
Each subagent needs its own retriable-versus-terminal handling, capped backoff, and fallback, so one stalled worker can't block synthesis.
The fan-out is too wide; reducing it to two subagents keeps traffic under the rate limit, so per-worker error handling becomes unnecessary.
Subagents share one retry budget with the lead, so the lead's SDK retries should have covered the worker's 429 automatically.

questions.explanation: The course warns that spreading work across agents multiplies the places a failure can happen. Each subagent needs the same retriable-versus-terminal handling, backoff, and fallback as a single agent, applied independently; one subagent that hits a rate limit with no backoff can stall the whole compilation step. Orchestration does not replace failure handling, it multiplies it.

distractor_explanations.A: Model capability does not add the missing retry and fallback logic to each worker.
distractor_explanations.C: Fewer workers lowers load, but each one still has no error handling.
distractor_explanations.D: Each subagent's calls are independent. The lead's retries do not cover a worker's calls.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team adds a cheap classifier call in front of every request to route between Haiku and Opus. Telemetry shows all traffic is the same short extraction shape, the classifier always picks Haiku, and Haiku holds the quality bar on the eval. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Keep the router as insurance in case harder requests appear later, because a single classifier call is negligible at any request volume.
Remove the router and pin one model; routing only pays off when traffic is mixed, and this traffic is uniform and met by Haiku.
Replace the classifier with Opus so routing decisions become more accurate, while continuing to send the routed requests to Haiku.
Route everything to Opus instead, because a uniform workload benefits most from the most capable model being applied consistently.

questions.explanation: A default model with an override, routed on a cheap signal, pays for the capable model only on requests that need it. The course is explicit about the flip side: when every request has the same shape, skip the router and pin one model. Routing adds a classification step and a second path to maintain, which uniform traffic never repays.

distractor_explanations.A: The classifier is an extra call on every request with no benefit. Add routing when traffic actually becomes mixed.
distractor_explanations.C: The decisions are already uniform, so a costlier router adds spend without changing any outcome.
distractor_explanations.D: The eval shows Haiku holds the bar, so stepping up adds cost with no need.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A procurement assistant receives free-form requests ranging from `find three suppliers for X` to `compare our last two contracts with Y and draft questions`. The goal and the tools (supplier search, contract retrieval, drafting) are clear, but the sequence changes with every request and cannot be enumerated. Actions are read-only or produce drafts, and non-determinism is acceptable. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A workflow with a router that classifies each request into one of a fixed set of enumerated branches, each with its own scripted steps.
A fixed prompt chain that always runs search, then retrieval, then drafting, skipping whichever steps a given request does not need.
A planner-executor-evaluator multi-agent system, because highly variable requests are best served by separate agents for planning and checking.
An agent: the goal and tools are clear but the path isn't, and the read-only, draft-producing toolset limits what the agent can actually do.

questions.explanation: The course's decision table says to choose an agent when you can specify the goal and tools but not the path, when user inputs vary unpredictably, when non-determinism is acceptable, and when the agent's actions are constrained by its registered toolset. Here every condition holds, and the read-only, draft-producing tools keep the risk low.

distractor_explanations.A: The request space does not reduce to a known set, so a workflow breaks when an input falls outside its branches.
distractor_explanations.B: The task needs creative sequencing of the tools. A fixed order cannot adapt as the path changes per request.
distractor_explanations.C: Multi-agent adds coordination cost. The course escalates only when a simpler pattern cannot handle the variability.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A reviewer audits an agent's wiring against the course's loop checklist. Which TWO findings are genuine defects? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The system prompt names the specific task and the tools available for it, rather than describing the agent's general capabilities.
The loop's only stopping rule is `stop_reason == "end_turn"`, with no iteration or budget cap if Claude keeps requesting tools.
The system prompt tells the agent to use `escalate_to_manager`, a tool that is not in the registered tools list.
Tool results are appended in a user-role turn rather than an assistant-role turn, even though the application produced them.
The loop returns a `tool_result` for every `tool_use` block in a turn before it sends the next request to the API.

questions.explanation: The course's loop wiring checklist requires that no unregistered tools be referenced in the system prompt, that the system prompt be scoped to the task and available tools, that every tool_use gets a tool_result before the next turn, that a HITL point is defined, and that exit conditions do not depend on Claude volunteering to stop. Referencing an unregistered tool and having no hard stop are the two violations here.

distractor_explanations.A: Scoping the system prompt to the task and its tools is exactly what the checklist recommends.
distractor_explanations.D: `tool_result` blocks always go in the user role. That is correct.
distractor_explanations.E: That is required behavior, not a defect.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer tries to create an agent resource on Claude Managed Agents and then start a session. Every call is rejected, even though the payloads match the documented shapes. Which omission is the most likely cause?

options.text: The `managed-agents-2026-04-01` beta header, which every Managed Agents endpoint requires while the product is in public beta.
The `code-execution-2025-08-25` header, because Managed Agents run their tools inside the code execution container used by skills.
The `mcp-client-2025-11-20` header, because every Managed Agent reaches its tools through the MCP connector by default.
A `settingSources` value, because the hosted loop needs to know which filesystem sources to load before a session can start.

questions.explanation: Claude Managed Agents is in public beta, and the course states that all of its endpoints require the `managed-agents-2026-04-01` beta header and that behavior may change between releases, so teams should build with a migration plan. The code-execution, skills, and mcp-client headers enable other API features, and `settingSources` belongs to the Agent SDK.

distractor_explanations.B: That header belongs to code execution and skills on the Messages API. Managed Agents have their own beta header.
distractor_explanations.C: The mcp-client header enables the API MCP connector's toolset, not the Managed Agents endpoints.
distractor_explanations.D: `settingSources` is an Agent SDK setting. Managed Agents have no filesystem discovery step.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A coaching agent holds months-long conversations with each user. Replaying the full stored history into every new session would outgrow the context budget well before the relationship ends, yet the agent must keep the gist of each user's goals and past commitments. Which memory scope does the course match to this, and what does it depend on?

options.text: In-context memory on a model with a larger window, because 1M-token windows remove the need for any memory strategy in long relationships.
Summarized memory injected at each session start; it depends on a well-specified summarizer prompt, because anything the summary drops is gone.
External storage that replays the full stored transcript at each session start, because persisting everything means no detail is ever lost.
Stateless sessions, because asking users to restate their goals each time keeps every session cheap, short, and independent of the last.

questions.explanation: The course's memory table lists summarized memory for long-running conversational agents whose full history would outgrow the context budget. It costs fewer tokens than replaying history but loses whatever the summarizer drops, so it depends on a summarizer prompt that names what to keep. External storage persists state, but replaying all of it into context does not solve a budget problem.

distractor_explanations.A: In-context state ends with the session, and cost grows with length. A bigger window postpones the problem rather than solving it.
distractor_explanations.C: Replaying the full history still puts all of it in context, which is the overflow the scenario rules out.
distractor_explanations.D: The agent has to carry commitments across sessions, and stateless memory loses all prior context.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A data-migration agent first produces a 40-step migration plan, then executes the steps with tools that each validate their own output. In two incidents every step succeeded, but the plan itself was wrong: it migrated the wrong tenant. Where does the course place the human-in-the-loop checkpoint that addresses this risk?

options.text: At the end of execution, where an operator compares the migrated data with the source before the migration is marked complete.
After the planning step and before execution begins, because a wrong plan fails even when every individual step executes correctly.
Inside each step's validation function, which should be extended to check tenant IDs against the plan before each step is committed.
On unexpected output only, because a tool returning an error flag or an empty result is the signal that the plan has gone wrong.

questions.explanation: The course's HITL table names three insertion points: before a destructive tool call (high, irreversible risk), after a planning step (medium risk: an incorrect plan produces the wrong outcome even if all steps execute correctly), and on unexpected output (failures retries won't fix). A plan-level error is caught only by a checkpoint on the plan itself.

distractor_explanations.A: Reviewing after execution comes too late; the wrong tenant has already been migrated.
distractor_explanations.C: Validation checks steps against the plan. If the plan is wrong, every step still passes, which is the scoped-exit-condition trap.
distractor_explanations.D: Every step succeeded here, so there was no unexpected output to trigger a check.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A parent agent delegates codebase exploration to a subagent so the main context stays small. Which TWO statements describe this handoff correctly? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The parent loses visibility into how the subagent reached its conclusion, since intermediate steps are discarded with its context.
The subagent automatically inherits the parent's full conversation history, so the task description given to it can be kept brief.
The subagent should get a scoped task, the minimum relevant context, the tools it needs, and exit conditions, and return a summary.
Handoffs reduce total token spend, so they should be the default for multi-step tasks even when the session never nears its context limit.
The subagent shares the parent's context window, so its exploration still counts against the parent's budget but is hidden from the transcript.

questions.explanation: A subagent handoff spawns an agent in its own isolated context window with only the task description and context it needs, and it returns a summary. The course lists what to pass (a scoped task, minimum relevant context, the tools, clear exit conditions) and what you give up (visibility into the intermediate steps, discarded with the subagent's context). Apply it where context cost is a real constraint.

distractor_explanations.B: Subagents start clean and must be given the context they need.
distractor_explanations.D: Handoffs add overhead. The course reserves them for cases where context cost is a real constraint.
distractor_explanations.E: Each subagent runs in its own isolated context window.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team needs to extract five fields from short, well-formatted shipping notices. A prototype planner-executor-evaluator multi-agent system works, but it is slow and expensive. What does the course's progression advise?

options.text: Start with the simplest pattern that works, a single well-constrained API call, and move up only when it can't handle the variability.
Collapse the three agents into one agent loop holding all three roles' tools, which keeps the flexibility while cutting the coordination cost.
Convert it to a workflow that chains the planner, executor, and evaluator as three fixed LLM calls in sequence for every notice.
Keep the multi-agent system but move every agent to the cheapest tier, because the architecture is sound and only the per-call model cost is too high.

questions.explanation: The course's progression is explicit: start with the simplest pattern that solves the problem (a single API call), then a workflow, then an agent, and move up only when the simpler pattern cannot handle the variability the task requires. Agents add behavioral complexity and multi-agent systems add coordination cost, neither of which a fixed-format extraction needs.

distractor_explanations.B: That is still an agent where a single call is enough. Agents are the last step in the progression.
distractor_explanations.C: Better than multi-agent, but three chained calls still over-build a task that one constrained call handles.
distractor_explanations.D: The architecture is the over-build. Extraction from well-formatted input does not need multiple agents.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A support agent was given 38 tools "just in case," many with overlapping descriptions. Selection quality has degraded, and the agent sometimes chains irrelevant tools together. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Keep all 38 tools and lengthen each description to several paragraphs, so Claude has more signal to separate one tool from the others.
Start from the minimum tool set the task actually needs, and add a tool only when a specific capability gap has been confirmed.
Split the 38 tools across four subagents at random, so that each subagent only has to choose among a smaller set of tools.
Keep all 38 tools and turn on extended thinking at high effort, so the model can reason more carefully over the larger tool set.

questions.explanation: The course says over-tooling is the more common production problem: teams register every tool they might need, and Claude's selection quality degrades as the tool surface grows, especially with overlapping descriptions. The remedy is to start with the minimum set the task needs and add a tool only when a specific capability gap is confirmed.

distractor_explanations.A: Overly long descriptions bury the trigger conditions, and the tool surface itself is still too large.
distractor_explanations.C: Random partitioning does not match tools to tasks. The fix is a minimal set chosen for the task.
distractor_explanations.D: Reasoning does not fix over-tooling. It adds cost while the overlap remains.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A system prompt says `Return JSON with fields order_id, items, and total.` `order_id` and `total` are always right, but the shape of `items` changes from run to run: sometimes objects with `sku` and `qty`, sometimes nested arrays, sometimes plain strings. Claude clearly understood the task. Which technique does the course's diagnosis table point to?

options.text: Few-shot examples showing the exact `items` structure, because the task is understood but the structure is being invented.
A more specific system prompt that restates the assistant's role as an order processor and lists the scope of what it should handle.
Extended thinking, so the model plans the full JSON structure step by step before it begins writing the response.
Rewording the field instruction to `Return valid JSON with correct items` and adding a closing reminder to keep the format consistent.

questions.explanation: The diagnosis table distinguishes a wrong shape (missing output constraint), content or scope drift (underspecified system prompt), and a correct task with invented structure, which calls for few-shot examples. Examples show the pattern rather than describe it, and one correct input-output pair pins down a structure that a written instruction leaves ambiguous. A schema-level constraint is the API-side complement.

distractor_explanations.B: Role or scope drift is not the symptom here. The content is correct, and only the structure is invented.
distractor_explanations.C: Reasoning depth does not fix structure. Examples or a schema constraint do.
distractor_explanations.D: Rephrasing does not add the missing structural piece, and the course warns that rewording rarely fixes this kind of failure.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer in a long Claude Code session has to choose context strategies. Which TWO pairings are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use `/compact` to switch to an unrelated task, because compaction removes the old task's context entirely before the new work starts.
Use `/compact` when nearing the context ceiling while continuing the same feature, accepting that details missing from the summary are lost.
Use `/clear` when switching to an unrelated task, after recording anything that must persist, such as a project convention, in CLAUDE.md.
Use `/clear` in the middle of a feature to cut cost, because Claude Code restores the cleared conversation automatically at the next prompt.
Prune by rewinding to an earlier message even when the work after that point holds discoveries the next step depends on.

questions.explanation: The course's four strategies trade continuity differently. Pruning rewinds and loses everything after the rewind point. Compaction (`/compact`) summarizes history to keep working on the same feature, at the cost of details the summary drops. Clearing (`/clear`) starts fresh for an unrelated task, so anything that must persist goes somewhere durable like CLAUDE.md. Subagent handoffs isolate exploratory work.

distractor_explanations.A: Compaction carries a summary forward, which brings bias from the previous task into unrelated work.
distractor_explanations.D: Clearing discards the session context, and nothing is restored afterward.
distractor_explanations.E: Pruning discards everything after the rewind point, including those discoveries.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: Over several iterations, a classifier prompt grew from 400 to 2,600 tokens of descriptive guidance. Accuracy stayed flat, but responses grew to over 2,000 characters and latency rose sharply. What mechanism and fix does the course identify?

options.text: Long prompts slow time to first token in proportion to their length, so the fix is to cache the 2,600-token prompt rather than shorten it.
Verbose output shows the model reasoning more carefully, so enabling extended thinking would move that reasoning out of the visible answer.
More responses are hitting `max_tokens`, so the fix is to raise `max_tokens`, which lets the longer responses finish sooner than they do now.
The model matches response length and style to its input, so a verbose prompt yields verbose output; use a constraint plus two examples.

questions.explanation: In the course's six-pass trace, pass 5 is the engineering failure: a verbose prompt produced verbose output of over 2,000 characters per call, because the model calibrates response length and style to its input, so latency rose with no accuracy gain. Pass 6 fixed it by replacing the descriptions with a structural constraint and two examples, which brought latency back down.

distractor_explanations.A: Caching cuts input processing, but this regression is output length driven by the verbose prompt. The content fix is a constraint plus examples.
distractor_explanations.B: Thinking adds billed tokens and does not address the verbosity the prompt induces.
distractor_explanations.C: Raising `max_tokens` allows longer output. It neither shortens responses nor reduces latency.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: `get_cached_result` is described as `Only use this if search_knowledge_base was called earlier in this conversation for the same query.` After the team adds aggressive pruning of older turns, Claude starts re-running `search_knowledge_base` for queries it has already searched. Why?

options.text: After pruning, the descriptions are too long relative to the remaining context, so they outweigh the user's message during tool routing.
Tool descriptions are cached at session start, so the pruned turns must be replayed before the descriptions are loaded and applied again.
Conditions that reference earlier turns can only be checked against history that is sent; pruning removed the evidence, so the rule fails silently.
Pruning changed the prompt-cache prefix, which invalidated the results `get_cached_result` had stored on Anthropic's servers for those queries.

questions.explanation: The course's exclusion-condition example comes with an explicit caveat: these conditions rely on complete conversation history being passed in each request, and if prior turns are truncated or dropped, Claude cannot evaluate them and the exclusion logic silently fails. Context strategies have to keep, for example in a compacted summary, any state the routing rules depend on.

distractor_explanations.A: Length is not the issue. The conditions point to turns that are no longer in the request.
distractor_explanations.B: Descriptions are sent with each request. The problem is the missing history the rule depends on.
distractor_explanations.D: `get_cached_result` is the application's own tool. Prompt-cache invalidation has no effect on tool data or routing logic.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A warehouse-safety tool sends photos with the prompt `Describe hazards in this image.` The output is shallow and inconsistent, especially where pallets overlap or a forklift is partly hidden behind racking. Which prompt change does the course recommend?

options.text: Give the prompt a target structure and say how to handle ambiguity, e.g. describe overlapping objects separately and flag occluded ones.
Send the same photo three times in one request, so the model can cross-check its own descriptions and resolve conflicts between them.
Send each photo at a higher resolution, so the model can resolve overlapping objects without any additional instructions in the prompt.
Turn on extended thinking, so the model reasons about depth, overlap, and occlusion before it writes its description of the hazards.

questions.explanation: The course says the same prompting techniques apply to images and PDFs: a bare "describe this image" prompt is shallow because Claude has no target structure. Images also carry ambiguity text lacks, such as overlapping objects, depth, and occlusion, so a visual prompt should state how to handle each case, for example "if objects overlap, describe each separately and note the overlap."

distractor_explanations.B: Duplicating the image multiplies visual tokens without supplying the missing structure.
distractor_explanations.C: Resolution does not tell the model how to report ambiguity, and larger images cost more tokens and may be downscaled anyway.
distractor_explanations.D: The missing piece is an explicit constraint for the ambiguity, the same diagnosis as with text prompts.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A compliance team requires that personal data never be stored in conversation logs, so a developer rewrites the text of thinking blocks to mask customer names before sending the history back during a tool-use loop. The API starts rejecting those requests. What is the correct resolution?

options.text: Mask the names and then recompute the signature on the client using the API key, so the modified thinking block still verifies.
Drop the thinking blocks from history entirely, because the signature check applies only when a thinking block is actually present.
Return thinking blocks exactly as received, since signatures verify them; meet the policy by masking thinking content in the app's own logs.
Convert the masked thinking blocks into `redacted_thinking` blocks, which the API accepts even when their content has been modified.

questions.explanation: The carry-back rule is structural: with extended thinking and tools, every thinking block, and every redacted thinking block, must go back to the API exactly as it arrived, because each carries a signature that proves it was not tampered with. Editing, summarizing, or dropping blocks breaks the next request. Data-handling requirements belong in what the application chooses to log or display.

distractor_explanations.A: Signatures are produced by the API, and the client cannot re-sign modified reasoning.
distractor_explanations.B: In a tool-use loop the thinking blocks must be passed back; dropping them also breaks the request.
distractor_explanations.D: Redacted thinking blocks are encrypted by the API and must also be returned unchanged. You cannot create them from edited text.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A `search_flights` tool marks `origin`, `destination`, `date`, `cabin_class`, and `max_price` all as required. Users often leave out cabin and budget, and traces show Claude filling in `economy` and arbitrary prices that silently filter out valid results. What is the fix?

options.text: Change `cabin_class` and `max_price` to type `null`, so Claude sends null when it is unsure and the function falls back to its own defaults.
Remove `cabin_class` and `max_price` from `required` and give them defaults in the function, so Claude can omit what it doesn't know.
Mark only `origin` as required, keeping the schema as permissive as possible so Claude has the most freedom when building each call.
Keep all five fields required and add `never guess values` to the description, so Claude asks the user before every call instead of guessing.

questions.explanation: The course's schema guidance is to mark a field required only when the call doesn't make sense without it. Marking everything required forces Claude to fabricate values for fields it has no basis to fill. Optional parameters with sensible defaults in the function signature let Claude leave out what it doesn't know, instead of guessing values that quietly change results.

distractor_explanations.A: That removes the ability to pass a real value. Optional fields with defaults are the pattern.
distractor_explanations.C: Destination and date are needed for the call to make sense. Required means non-negotiable, not minimal.
distractor_explanations.D: Required fields force a value on every call. The schema, not an instruction, is the lever here.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: After a tool-selection bug, a team expands every tool description to about 600 words covering implementation history, edge-case lore, and internal ticket numbers. Selection accuracy gets worse. Which guidance from the course explains this?

options.text: Keep descriptions to three or four sentences on what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns; excess detail buries the triggers.
Tool descriptions carry less weight than the input schema, so the added prose is ignored and the regression must come from somewhere else.
Descriptions are cut off after a fixed character limit, so the trigger conditions written at the end of each long description are never seen.
Long descriptions are fine; the regression simply shows that the tools must now be merged into one tool that takes a type parameter.

questions.explanation: The course's decision table puts description length at three to four sentences per tool, covering what it does, when Claude should reach for it, and what it returns, with examples where format matters. Too short and Claude guesses; too long and the trigger conditions get buried under detail Claude doesn't use when it decides which tool to call.

distractor_explanations.B: Descriptions are weighed heavily in routing. Adding noise degraded the very signal Claude uses.
distractor_explanations.C: The course's concern is that useful signal gets buried, not that descriptions are truncated.
distractor_explanations.D: Merging is for tools whose descriptions cannot be separated. Here the descriptions were bloated, not overlapping.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team reaches a large MCP server through the API's MCP Connector and also uses the same server in Claude Code. In the API integration, the model must never see the admin tools. In Claude Code, `mcp__crm__update_contact` should run without a prompt and `mcp__crm__delete_contact` should be blocked. Which combination is right?

options.text: In the API, add deny permission rules for the admin tools; in Claude Code, set `enabled: false` on `delete_contact` in the project's `.mcp.json`.
In both integrations, set `defer_loading: true` on the admin and delete tools, so those tools never load and therefore can never execute.
API: `enabled: false` for the admin tools in `mcp_toolset` configs. Claude Code: allow `mcp__crm__update_contact`, deny `mcp__crm__delete_contact`.
In both integrations, add a CLAUDE.md instruction listing the forbidden tools, since one written convention can cover both runtimes at once.

questions.explanation: The course separates two controls. In Claude Code, permission rules can name a single MCP tool as `mcp__server__tool`: an allow skips its prompt, and a deny blocks it while other tools still prompt. With the API MCP Connector, the `enabled` flag in `mcp_toolset` decides whether the model sees a tool at all. One is a governance control and the other a scope and context-cost control, and they are often used together.

distractor_explanations.A: This is reversed: `enabled` is the connector's visibility control, and permission rules are Claude Code's run-governance control.
distractor_explanations.B: `defer_loading` delays loading until the tool is needed. It neither hides nor blocks the tool.
distractor_explanations.D: CLAUDE.md is not enforcement, and it does not apply to API requests at all.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer is choosing configuration scopes for MCP servers in Claude Code. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enterprise scope requires every developer to run an add command once before the administrator's servers appear in their sessions.
Local scope stores the server in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which is git-ignored, making it the right scope for team-shared servers.
A project-scoped stdio server in `.mcp.json` spawns a subprocess on each teammate's machine, so each needs the runtime installed.
User scope writes the server into the repository's `.mcp.json`, so the configuration follows the user into every clone of every project.
Local scope stores the server in `~/.claude.json` under the current project's path, applying to that project only and not shared.

questions.explanation: The course defines four MCP scopes. Local is `~/.claude.json` under the current project's path, personal to one project. User is personal settings across all projects. Project is `.mcp.json` at the repository root, shared through version control; a stdio server configured there launches a local subprocess on each clone. Enterprise is admin-managed and pushed to every user.

distractor_explanations.A: Enterprise scope pushes servers to all users without any individual configuration steps.
distractor_explanations.B: Local MCP scope lives in `~/.claude.json` per project. Team-shared servers belong in project scope.
distractor_explanations.D: User scope lives in personal settings across projects and is not written into any repository.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer connects twelve MCP servers in Claude Code and worries that hundreds of tool definitions will fill the context window before any work begins. What does Claude Code do by default?

options.text: It caps the number of connected servers at five per session and silently ignores the remaining servers until earlier ones disconnect.
It loads every connected server's tool definitions at session start, so the developer must disconnect servers to stay within the budget.
It defers definitions and searches for the tools a task needs; an opt-in mode loads them upfront when they fit in about 10% of the window.
It loads all definitions upfront but marks them with prompt caching, so after the first request they no longer occupy any context.

questions.explanation: Per the course, Claude Code by default defers MCP tool definitions and uses a search step to discover and load only the tools a task needs; an opt-in mode loads definitions upfront when they fit within about 10 percent of the context window. Every connected server still adds to the pool the model must account for, so connect only what the work needs.

distractor_explanations.A: There is no such cap. Connecting only the servers you need is still good practice.
